common_name: Pee Dee Ingot Lilyturf (Golden Lily Turf)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Pee Dee Ingot's short rhizomes keep it in a tight, non-spreading clump, so give plants their full 12-18 inch spread before crowding in new divisions.

directions: Pee Dee Ingot is a compact, clump-forming liriope selected for solid gold to chartreuse-yellow foliage rather than the green or white-striped leaves of other muscari cultivars in this collection; the color is brightest with several hours of direct sun and mellows toward yellow-green in deeper shade. Unlike Variegata or Gold Band, which pair green leaves with cream stripes, Pee Dee Ingot's blades are uniformly colored, giving a bolder, more solid-looking accent in border plantings. Short, tight rhizomes keep the clump neat and slow to spread, and lavender flower spikes appear in late summer mostly hidden within the foliage. Named for the Pee Dee River region of the Carolinas where it was selected, it is prized for brightening dark corners and pairing with dark-leaved companions such as black mondo grass.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in light, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Royal Purple is grown as a clumping accent for its unusually dark flower spikes rather than variegated foliage.

directions: Royal Purple is a clumping liriope selected for flower color rather than foliage pattern: its densely packed spikes open a deep violet-purple, noticeably darker and richer than the lavender-purple of Big Blue or the white blooms of Monroe White, giving the strongest floral impact of any muscari cultivar in this collection. The strap-like leaves stay a plain, glossy dark green all season, without the cream or gold variegation seen in Variegata, Gold Band, or Pee Dee Ingot, so the plant reads as a clean green backdrop until the flower spikes emerge in late summer. Like other clumping liriope, it holds its footprint tightly rather than spreading by runners, making it dependable for formal edging. Shiny black berries follow the flowers and persist into winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Silver Dragon spreads by stolons like the parent species but noticeably less aggressively, and its white-striped leaves show best with a few hours of direct or bright filtered light.

directions: Silver Dragon is a variegated sport of creeping lilyturf, its narrow, quarter-inch-wide leaves striped lengthwise in silvery white and green rather than the solid dark green of the straight species, giving a brighter, cooler-toned groundcover mat. It spreads by stolons and will still colonize an area over time, but less aggressively and slightly shorter than plain Liriope spicata, making it more manageable in smaller beds. The variegation reportedly comes with useful resistance to the leaf-spot fungal disease that can disfigure other variegated liriopes in humid climates. Pale lilac-white flower spikes in late summer are followed by black berries, though the striped foliage remains the main ornamental draw.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Little Tabby Dwarf Variegated Mondo Grass

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Little Tabby is slower and smaller-growing than green mondo grass, so use closer spacing and be patient while young plantings knit together.

directions: Little Tabby is a dwarf, variegated sport of black mondo grass, but unlike the solid near-black leaves of 'Nigrescens', its narrow blades stay dark green edged in fine, silvery-white margins, giving a subtly frosted, two-toned effect rather than the dramatic dark foliage the species is known for. At only two to three inches tall it forms one of the smallest mondo grass mats in cultivation, useful for miniature gardens, trough plantings, and tight gaps between pavers where full-sized mondo would overwhelm the scale. Growth is slow even by mondo grass standards, and clumps are best left undisturbed for several years before dividing. Inconspicuous pale flowers and dark berries appear occasionally but are secondary to the foliage effect.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Little Rev Flax Lily (Dwarf Spreading Flax Lily)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Rev's compact, dwarf habit makes it useful for smaller borders and mass planting where standard-sized flax lilies would be too large.

directions: Little Rev is a dwarf selection of the Australian spreading flax lily, staying under 16 inches tall and wide — roughly half the size of Blue Flax Lily (Dianella caerulea) already in this collection — with narrow, arching, blue-gray-green foliage that reads more silvery than the plain green blades of Tasman Flax Lily. Pale blue to violet, star-shaped flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring, followed by indigo-blue berries that persist into fall. Its small, tidy clumping habit and drought tolerance make it well suited to mass planting along verges, rockeries, and roundabouts where a compact, low-water groundcover is needed. It tolerates a wide range of light from full sun to fairly deep shade.
sources: UC Landscape Plant Irrigation Trials (UC Davis)
Botanic Gardens of South Australia — Plant Selector

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to moist, salt-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade; Cassa Blue holds a tighter, more upright, phormium-like clump than the species and needs less frequent grooming.

directions: Cassa Blue is a hybrid flax lily selection (Dianella caerulea crossed with D. longifolia) bred for dense, upright, silvery blue-gray foliage that holds its color more consistently than the greener-toned species already in this collection. Its stiff, sword-like leaves form a tighter, more architectural clump than straight Blue Flax Lily, spreading wider than tall. Violet, star-shaped flowers with gold anthers appear on branching stems above the foliage in mid-spring, followed by an abundance of glossy royal-blue berries in early summer. It is notably salt- and drought-tolerant once established, making it a good choice for coastal and roadside plantings as well as shaded borders.

common_name: Variegated Flax Lily (White-Striped Tasman Flax Lily)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, average to moist soil in partial to full shade; keep Variegata out of hot, direct afternoon sun, which can scorch the white leaf margins.

directions: Variegata is a striped sport of Tasman Flax Lily, its long, arching, strap-shaped leaves edged in crisp white rather than the solid dark green of the species, giving a much brighter, more luminous presence in shaded beds. Lavender, star-shaped flowers with a soft sky-blue cast appear on tall stems in mid-spring, followed by the same shining royal-blue berries that make Dianella tasmanica such a distinctive plant, held against the pale-edged foliage. It forms the same dense, spreading, evergreen clumps as the parent species but is best kept out of intense afternoon sun, which can bleach or scorch the white margins. A favorite for lighting up deep shade under trees where dark-leaved groundcovers would otherwise look flat.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, drier clay to average soil in full sun to partial shade; spreading flax lily is markedly more drought- and frost-tolerant than the other Dianella species in this collection and needs little supplemental water once established.

directions: Spreading flax lily is an Australian species distinguished from Blue Flax Lily and Tasman Flax Lily by its brown to black (rather than yellow) anthers and its tolerance of drier, harder clay soils and colder conditions, including light frost and snow. It forms upright, rhizomatous clumps of narrow, stiff, dark-green strap leaves and produces loose sprays of deep blue to purple, star-shaped flowers from spring into summer, followed by shiny blue, egg-shaped berries. Because it spreads gradually by rhizome, mature plantings knit into a continuous, weed-suppressing groundcover in woodland and dry shade settings. It is notably tougher and more cold-hardy than the more commonly planted Dianella caerulea and D. tasmanica, extending the useful range of flax lilies into cooler zones.
sources: Australian National Botanic Gardens — Growing Native Plants
Plant Selector — Botanic Gardens of South Australia
